scenes.heading: Pythagoras’ theorem
scenes.sub: Know two sides? Find the third!
scenes.say: How long does a ladder need to be? How big is a TV screen across the diagonal? In any right-angled triangle, if you know two sides you can find the third, using Pythagoras' theorem.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Build a square tile on each side of the triangle
scenes.science: Two small tiles = the big tile: 9 + 16 = 25 for sides 3, 4, 5
scenes.breaks: It only works for right-angled triangles. On any other triangle the two small tiles won't add up to the big one.
scenes.say: Picture a right-angled triangle with a square tile built on each side. The two small tiles together have the same area as the big tile on the longest side. With sides three, four and five, nine plus sixteen equals twenty-five.
scenes.caption: Build a square on each side. The two small squares add up to the big one. Sides 3, 4, 5: 9 + 16 = 25.

scenes.heading: Squares on the sides
notes: Small squares add to the big one
scenes.say: Here it is drawn out. First the triangle with sides three, four and five. Then a square on each side. Nine plus sixteen makes twenty-five, the square on the hypotenuse.

scenes.heading: Pythagoras’ theorem
scenes.say: Here's the rule. c squared equals a squared plus b squared. c is the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle. a and b are the two shorter sides.
scenes.caption: c² = a² + b². c is the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle. a and b are the shorter sides.

scenes.heading: Spot the hypotenuse
notes: c is the side opposite it
scenes.say: Always find the right angle first. The hypotenuse, c, is the side across from it. It never touches the little square, and it's always the longest side.

scenes.heading: Find the hypotenuse
scenes.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
scenes.say: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides six and eight centimetres. Square them: thirty-six and sixty-four. Add: one hundred. Then square root. The hypotenuse is ten centimetres.
scenes.caption: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100. √100 = 10. The hypotenuse is 10 cm.

scenes.heading: TV screen
scenes.question: A TV screen is 80 cm wide and 45 cm high. Find its diagonal, to 1 decimal place.
scenes.say: A TV is eighty centimetres wide and forty-five high. The diagonal is the hypotenuse. Eighty squared plus forty-five squared is eight thousand four hundred and twenty-five. The square root is about ninety-one point eight centimetres.
scenes.caption: 80² + 45² = 6400 + 2025 = 8425. √8425 ≈ 91.8 cm.

scenes.heading: Square, add, square root
steps: Find the right angle; label c opposite it
scenes.say: So the method is: find the right angle and label the hypotenuse opposite it. Square the two shorter sides. Add them to get c squared. Then take the square root. Square, add, square root.

scenes.heading: Handy facts
points: If a² + b² = c², it's a right angle
c is longer than a or b, less than a + b
scenes.say: Some whole-number sets fit exactly, like three four five, five twelve thirteen and eight fifteen seventeen. The rule also works backwards: if a squared plus b squared equals c squared, the triangle has a right angle.
scenes.caption: Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17. If a² + b² = c², the triangle has a right angle.

points: Check: c is the longest side
scenes.say: Quick recap. Pythagoras works in right-angled triangles. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. c squared equals a squared plus b squared, so square, add, square root. And check that c is the longest side. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Right-angled triangles only. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. c² = a² + b²: square, add, square root. Check c is the longest side. Now try the practice questions!
